sections.h2: Every brief starts with 30 minutes of somebody's actual time
body: Here's the uncomfortable bit, up front: if the only input to your content is the ten pages already ranking, you will produce the eleventh version of those ten pages. Google has spent three years getting better at spotting exactly that, and the AI answer sitting above the results has made the eleventh version worthless anyway.

So we do the annoying thing. Before a brief exists, we record a 30-minute call with someone inside your business who knows something we don't. What comes out of it is the reason the piece exists — a number, an objection, a failure mode, a thing customers get wrong that nobody has bothered to write down.
Who we need depends on the piece. It's rarely marketing.
bullets: **Founder or head of sales** for anything about pricing, objections, or why deals are lost. Fifteen minutes here beats a week of research.
**Support or customer success** for how-to and troubleshooting content. They know the exact wording customers use, which is also the exact wording customers search.
**Delivery, engineering or clinical staff** for anything technical. One specific caveat from someone who does the work is worth 400 words of hedging.
**Nobody at all** for glossary entries and definitional pages — those genuinely can be desk-researched, and we don't waste your team's time pretending otherwise.

callout.title: What the 30 minutes actually costs you
callout.body: One recorded call per two or three pieces, batched into a single hour a fortnight. We send the questions 48 hours ahead. You don't prepare, you don't write anything, and you never see a Google Doc asking you to "add your thoughts here".

sections.h2: Where we use AI, and where it's banned
body: Every agency in India now says "AI-assisted". Almost none of them will tell you where the line sits, so here's ours, in specifics.

Google's own position is that it doesn't care how content is produced, only whether it's useful and original. That's true, and it's also widely misread. Content that's useful because a human who does the work explained something clears the bar easily. Content spun from the same public sources everyone else used clears nothing, whichever tool produced it. See [does AI content hurt SEO](/answers/does-ai-content-hurt-seo) for the longer argument.

body: Saying no is most of what makes this work, and it's the part clients find irritating in month one and defend in month eight.
bullets: **Volume briefs with no source.** "Forty articles on generic industry topics" is a request to produce forty pages nobody will read. We'll counter with twelve that have something in them.

**Keywords with no business behind them.** High volume, zero intent to buy, ranked by five publishers with twenty times your authority. We'll show you the maths and suggest something narrower and winnable.
**Pages your product can't back up.** If the article promises something your onboarding doesn't do, the content converts and then churns. That's worse than not ranking.
**Anything requiring an invented statistic.** If we can't source it to a real, nameable study, it doesn't go in. This costs us headlines and we're fine with that.
**Rewriting a competitor's post more thoroughly.** That's the definition of the eleventh version. If the only differentiator is length, there's no differentiator.

sections.h2: How the 90-day guarantee applies to content
body: The company guarantee is a single frozen number: your trailing-90-day count of qualified leads from organic search, recorded on day one. If we haven't beaten it inside 90 days, we keep working free until we do. That applies whether you're on [SEO](/seo), [organic social and content](/social), or both.

Content is where that promise is hardest, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. A brand-new pillar page published in month one often peaks in month six or later — that's not underperformance, that's how the index works. Anyone telling you new content ranks in three weeks is describing a keyword nobody competes for.

So when the guarantee is on the clock, we sequence for it. Refreshes on pages already sitting in positions 5–15 come first, because those move fastest and often move within weeks. Cannibalising pages get merged. Pages that convert but don't rank get the internal links they should have had. Net-new pillar content still ships, but it's building the second and third quarter, not the first.

Alongside the leads number we freeze two content-specific baselines on day one: organic sessions to non-branded pages, and assisted conversions from organic content in your analytics. Those tell you whether the content is working well before the revenue does. What we won't do is promise a position for a keyword — the guarantee is always against your own starting numbers, never against Google's index.

faqs.q: How much do content marketing services cost in India?
faqs.a: Ours run ₹30,000–₹70,000 a month, ex-GST, for four to eight interview-led pieces plus strategy and reporting. The wider Indian market runs from ₹1.50 a word for bulk freelance output to ₹15,000+ per piece for research-led work. The gap is almost entirely whether a subject-matter expert was involved before the writing started.

faqs.q: Why do you insist on interviewing our team?
faqs.a: Because it's the only reliable source of something your competitors can't replicate from the same search results. Thirty minutes with your head of sales produces objections, numbers and failure modes that no amount of desk research surfaces. It's also what makes the content pass the experience half of E-E-A-T rather than just claiming to.

faqs.q: How many blog posts do we need per month?
faqs.a: Four a month, sustained for a year, beats fifty in one quarter followed by nothing — search rewards a site that keeps publishing and keeps updating. For a young site in a competitive category, eight a month gets you to a defensible topic cluster faster. Below four, you're maintaining rather than growing.

faqs.q: Do you use AI to write the content?
faqs.a: Not for drafts. AI handles research, query clustering, transcription and outline checks. A human writes from the interview transcript, a named editor verifies every factual claim, and no quote or statistic ever originates from a model. If you want cheap AI output at volume there are vendors for that, and we'd genuinely rather you used them than paid us to pretend.

faqs.q: How long until content starts driving traffic?
faqs.a: Refreshed pages that already rank can move within two to six weeks. New content on a competitive term typically takes three to six months to settle, and compounds after that. If someone promises new pages ranking in weeks, ask which keyword — it'll be one with no competition and no buyers.

faqs.q: Who owns the content you write?
faqs.a: You do — drafts, published pages, briefs and the raw interview recordings. There's no lock-in and no licensing arrangement where the work stops being yours when the retainer ends. Month-to-month after the first quarter, 30 days' notice, and everything is handed over on the way out.
